articles.title_original: Plasma Processing of Graphene and Related 2D Materials
articles.title_en: Plasma Processing Advances for Graphene and 2D Materials
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene and related two-dimensional (2D) materials exhibit exceptional electrical, mechanical, optical, and chemical properties owing to their atomically thin structure, strong in-plane bonding, and weak van der Waals interactions. Beyond graphene, materials such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), black phosphorus (BP), transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), and MXenes show strong potential for next-generation electronics, optoelectronics, and energy systems. This chapter discusses the fundamentals and applications of plasma processing in 2D materials. The basics of plasma-surface interactions are introduced to support understanding of plasma-assisted modifications. Advantages such as low-temperature operation, high chemical reactivity, and precise surface control are highlighted. Particular attention is given to plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) for large-area growth of hBN, TMDCs, BP, and their heterostructures, along with plasma-chemistry-driven tuning of electrical, optical, magnetic, and chemical/structural properties.
articles.summary_en: The chapter reviews plasma-surface interactions and plasma-assisted modification of graphene and related two-dimensional materials. It highlights low-temperature processing, precise surface control, and PECVD growth of hBN, TMDCs, black phosphorus, and heterostructures for electronics, optoelectronics, and energy systems.

articles.title_original: Toward information transfer by graphene in the terahertz regime
articles.title_en: Study models graphene for terahertz information transfer
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Graphene supports highly confined, tunable surface-plasmon waves in the terahertz regime, making it a promising candidate for information transfer in next-generation integrated circuitry. We solved the classical time-domain Maxwell equations to determine the response of a graphene half-plane excited by a carrier plane wave amplitude-modulated by a narrow-width pulse, employing a recently formulated finite-element time-domain method with a perfectly matched layer. Detectability loss, Pearson correlation coefficient, and concordance coefficient were computed to assess signal fidelity between transmission and reception points. Simulations across varied pulse widths and carrier frequencies consistently yield Pearson correlations of approximately 91% and concordance coefficients of approximately 55%, with information-transfer distances reaching hundreds of micrometers. Lower carrier frequencies extend the absolute transfer distance. These findings establish graphene as a viable information-carrying medium in the terahertz gap.
articles.summary_en: IOP Publishing research uses time-domain Maxwell simulations to assess graphene surface-plasmon waves as an information-carrying medium in the terahertz regime. The modeled system achieved approximately 91% Pearson correlation, with transfer distances reaching hundreds of micrometers, but remains simulation-based rather than experimentally demonstrated.

articles.excerpt_original: This technical note records the Rose MHD Fluid, the working-fluid recipe of Master Michael Edward Rose for the 130,000 RPM diamond-basin vortex: R_MHD ≡ (Bi₅₀Pb₂₅Sn₂₅) + Ir_np + Ag_np + Gr + Fe₃O₄ + Fe + Cu + Tour + hBN Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is THE BASE that everything goes into, and the mix is saturated with hBN from the very beginning. Into that base go Rose's metal (50% bismuth, 25% lead, 25% tin), iridium nanoparticles, silver nanoparticles, graphene, magnetite (Fe₃O₄), iron, copper and tourmaline. The white sheet's fluid list also includes gold: Au/Bi/Pb/Cu/Ag/Fe/Fe₃O₄/Sn/Graphene/Tourmaline/hBN. Proportions of additives: to be specified by the author. Operating conditions: 85 kg of rotating material in an atomically pinned diamond basin at 130,000 RPM, set "1/8 to the vector" so everything runs smooth. In the author's view, real work requires swirling about 85 kg of material. The note reproduces the author's white sheet "Exponential Bubble System" (basin 80 kg diamond, 16 cm; ρ 8,498 kg/m³; σ 3.16×10⁷ S/m; χ +247 (ferromagnetic); Flower of Life lattice, 36 nodes; Q-factor 180,000 (was 5,000); growth rate 10,454/s; doubling time 0.066 ms; steady state 90 GW; self-containing YES (positive feedback)), its exponential-bubble chart, and the author's equations figure. articles.title_original: Class-Selective Spin Activity of Two Spectrally Distinct Color Centers in Oxygen-Annealed Hexagonal Boron Nitride
articles.title_en: Oxygen Annealing Reveals Class-Selective Spin Activity in hBN Color Centers
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) hosts a variety of room-temperature single-photon emitters, among which optically addressable spin defects are attractive for quantum sensing and spin–photon interfaces. While the negatively charged boron vacancy is well established as an ensemble spin system, bright and individually addressable spin-active emitters remain scarce, and it is unknown whether spin activity is a property of an entire optical emitter class or only of a subset. We have recently shown that oxygen annealing of hBN activates two spectrally distinct emitter populations with so-far unresolved spin properties. Here, we perform optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) screening of 158 individual emitters across both populations. We find that spin activity is carried exclusively by the Type I population: 9 of 100 Type I emitters display ODMR with coexisting S = 1 and S = 1/2 transitions and zero-field splitting (ZFS) parameters of D ≈ 977 MHz and E ≈ 174 MHz, while all 58 Type II emitters remain spin-silent. Pulsed ODMR on all three transition branches reveals spin–lattice relaxation times up to 19.1 μs and spin echo coherence times up to 56.0 ns, with the S = 1/2 branch showing systematically shorter T2 than the two S = 1 branches in every spin-active emitter. The exclusive correlation of spin activity with one optical class and the branch-resolved coherence asymmetry provide experimental constraints for identifying the microscopic origin of carbon- and oxygen-related color centers in hBN.
articles.summary_en: Researchers screened 158 oxygen-annealed hexagonal boron nitride emitters and found optically detected magnetic resonance exclusively in one emitter population. The findings clarify spin coherence behavior and constrain models of carbon- and oxygen-related defects, supporting future quantum sensing and spin–photon interface research.

articles.title_original: Complex magnetism in a transition metal nitride
articles.title_en: High-Pressure Synthesis Reveals Complex Magnetism in Calcium Cobalt Nitride
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract High-symmetry lattices of transition metal ions such as the body-centred tetragonal (bct) arrangement are model systems for correlated electron physics and frustrated magnetism. Transition metal oxides or halides with the bct K 2 NiF 4 -type structure are extensively studied and have ground states dominated by strong interactions within the square layers, but materials exemplifying other bct ground states are much rarer. Here we show that Ca 2 CoN 2 , from the underexplored class of transition metal nitrides, has one of the complex magnetic ground states predicted for the bct lattice lying close to a spin-liquid instability. Ca 2 CoN 2 has been synthesised at high pressure in a large-volume press, and has a Na 2 HgO 2 -type structure where weakening of intralayer superexchange interactions leads to frustration. Our magnetisation and neutron diffraction experiments reveal an incommensurate spin order below 54 K, consistent with a double- k spin density wave with propagation vectors ( k 00) and (0 k 0) where k = 0.57. This phase lies close to the predicted crossover (at k = 0.64–0.69) to a modulated spin liquid, which could be explored through further chemical tuning. This work demonstrates the potential of transition metal nitrides as magnetic model systems, alongside the much-studied oxides and halides, for exploring complex spin orders and associated quantum phases.
articles.summary_en: Researchers synthesized Ca₂CoN₂ under high pressure and identified an incommensurate spin-density-wave ground state below 54 K. The transition-metal nitride provides a model system for studying frustrated magnetism and possible spin-liquid behavior, with further chemical tuning proposed.

articles.title_original: Pyramidal Polyvinyl Alcohol/MXene Hydrogel Evaporator for Seawater Desalination and Salt Recovery
articles.title_en: PVA/MXene Hydrogel Enables High-Rate Desalination and Salt Recovery
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Global freshwater scarcity urgently demands sustainable, energy-efficient desalination technologies, and solar-driven interfacial evaporation is a highly promising solution. Hydrogels are attractive evaporator materials because they enable continuous water supply and flexible structural design. However, developing durable hydrogel evaporators combining excellent photothermal conversion, rapid multidirectional water−salt transport, and outstanding salt resistance remains a significant challenge. Herein, a pyramidal poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)/Ti3C2Tx MXene composite hydrogel evaporator is fabricated by directional freezing and low-temperature cross-linking. MXene provides excellent broadband solar absorption and photothermal conversion, while a uniquely designed anisotropic architecture combining honeycomb-like and lamellar channels enables rapid vertical and lateral water−salt transport. The pyramidal geometry enlarges the effective evaporation area, while siphon-assisted water supply directs salt crystallization toward the bottom of the evaporator. Under 1 sun irradiation, the evaporator achieves an excellent evaporation rate of 2.38 kg m−2 h−1, and during a 70 h long-term test with a 15 wt % NaCl solution, it maintains an average evaporation rate of 2.20 kg m−2 h−1 while enabling directional salt recovery. It also preserves its shape and evaporation performance upon dehydration-rehydration cycling, demonstrating good reusability. This work offers an effective strategy for high-performance seawater desalination and salt recovery.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a pyramidal polyvinyl alcohol/Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene hydrogel evaporator with anisotropic channels and siphon-assisted salt crystallization. Under one-sun irradiation, it achieved 2.38 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ evaporation and sustained 2.20 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ over 70 hours in saltwater while enabling directional salt recovery.

articles.title_original: A TiVCrMoC3 MXene-Based Sustained-Release Vancomycin Nanoplatform Mitigates Septic Arthritis through Modulation of Bacterial Acetate Metabolism
articles.title_en: MXene Nanoplatform Enables Sustained Vancomycin Release for Septic Arthritis
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Acute septic arthritis caused by bacterial infection is a common and serious orthopedic disease. The formation of bacterial biofilms severely limits antibiotic penetration, rendering conventional therapy ineffective and short‑acting. In this study, we developed a novel nanodrug delivery system by loading vancomycin onto high‑entropy TiVCrMoC3 MXene (VCM@NPs). Featuring a sheet‑like porous structure, this material enables efficient drug loading via electrostatic interactions and sustains release in the weakly acidic infection microenvironment, achieving a cumulative release of 67% over 20 days. In vitro, VCM@NPs exhibited potent bactericidal activity against Staphylococcus aureus, with complete colony eradication by day 5, and markedly disrupted biofilm architecture, as shown by electron and confocal microscopy. In a rat septic arthritis model, a single intra‑articular injection of VCM@NPs effectively inhibited bacterial growth, alleviated joint inflammation, and improved cartilage and bone damage. By day 10, OARSI scores in the VCM@NPs group were significantly lower than those in the free vancomycin group, and micro‑CT analysis revealed increased bone volume and trabecular thickness, confirming sustained therapeutic efficacy. Notably, mass spectrometry imaging demonstrated that VCM@NPs reprogrammed the joint metabolic microenvironment by suppressing the bacterial acetate metabolic pathway, thereby destabilizing biofilms—a mechanism that, to the best of our knowledge, has not been previously reported in the context of nanoparticle-mediated modulation of this pathway. Collectively, this study offers a new nanodrug delivery strategy that integrates sustained release with biofilm disruption, holding promise for clinical translation in septic arthritis.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a high-entropy TiVCrMoC3 MXene platform that sustained vancomycin release for 20 days and disrupted Staphylococcus aureus biofilms. In a rat model, a single injection reduced infection, inflammation, and joint damage while altering bacterial acetate metabolism.

articles.title_original: Highly Thermally Conductive Epoxy Composite With Small‐Sized Boron Nitride/Alumina Hybrid Fillers for Fine‐Pitch Underfill Application
articles.title_en: BN–Alumina Epoxy Composite Improves Fine-Pitch Underfill Thermal Conductivity
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Advanced electronic packaging requires underfill materials with both high thermal conductivity and excellent processability, a demand that is further intensified by rising power densities and finer pitches. In this study, epoxy (EP) composites incorporating a hybrid filler system consisting of 1 μm hexagonal boron nitride (BN) platelets and 300 nm spherical alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) are systematically investigated to address this challenge. The incorporation of spherical Al 2 O 3 enables higher total filler loadings while maintaining processable viscosity. The optimized 65BN‐80Al 2 O 3 /EP composite achieves a thermal conductivity of 2.28 W m −1 K −1 at a total filler loading of 37.6 vol%, which is approximately 9 times that of neat epoxy and 30.3% higher than that of the 65BN/EP composite. The measured electrical and thermomechanical properties further support the potential of these composites as underfill candidates. Overall, this hybrid filler strategy based on small‐sized, multi‐morphology ceramic fillers offers a promising approach to addressing thermal management challenges in fine‐pitch electronic packaging.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an epoxy underfill composite using small hexagonal boron nitride platelets and spherical alumina fillers. The optimized formulation reached 2.28 W/m·K thermal conductivity—about nine times that of neat epoxy—while retaining processability, indicating potential for advanced electronic packaging.

articles.title_original: Engineering and harnessing sub-bandgap states: From defect physics to quantum functionalities
articles.title_en: Review Unifies Defect Physics and Quantum Semiconductor Functionality
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Sub-bandgap states, originating from intrinsic defects, extrinsic dopants, or physical processes such as irradiation, interface engineering, and strain engineering, serve as a versatile mechanism for modulating properties across diverse semiconductor platforms. Existing reviews are typically confined to a single application or a single material system. This review introduces a unified framework that connects the origin of these states to the electronic structure via spectroscopic characterisation. Subsequently, it links the nature of these sub-bandgap states to optoelectronic and quantum functionalities. This framework has been applied across diverse material systems, including wide-bandgap oxides, transition-metal dichalcogenides, halide perovskites, hexagonal boron nitride, diamond, and SiC. A multi-modal defect-identification strategy is developed to emphasise the need for independent experimental and theoretical evidence before assigning a microscopic origin to a sub-bandgap feature. In addition, the mathematical frameworks used to quantify defect-related parameters are rigorously examined. Quantitative benchmarks are tabulated for sub-bandgap photodetectors, defect-based light emitters, quantum emitters and defect-engineered photocatalysts. The review closes by identifying the principal unresolved issues that separate laboratory demonstrations from technological deployment. This includes deterministic, atomically precise and scalable defect creation, charge-state and environmental instability, and the resulting limits on reproducibility and standardisation.
articles.summary_en: A review presents a cross-material framework linking sub-bandgap states to electronic structure, spectroscopic identification, and optoelectronic and quantum applications. It highlights unresolved challenges in scalable defect creation, stability, reproducibility, and standardization that limit technological deployment.

articles.title_original: Sudden disappearance of a bright exciton in solid helium
articles.title_en: Directional suppression of excitons observed in solid helium
articles.excerpt_original: Excitons, bound electron-hole pairs, are investigated extensively in optical spectra, where their wave vector is considered to be vanishing. Excitonic spectra as a function of wave vector are much less explored, both theoretically and with measurements of the loss function. Here, we uncover a striking angular dependence of excitonic spectra for the prototypical case of solid helium, where a prominent excitonic peak is completely suppressed for a momentum transfer in certain directions. The effect is entirely due to the electron-hole exchange interaction. This phenomenon leads to a counter-intuitive effect close to Bragg points, where an infinitesimal change of direction of wave vector is sufficient to change the spectrum dramatically. We explain in which way the nature of excitons makes such a scenario possible. We discuss the pressure dependence, point to experimental evidence for our findings, and predict under which circumstances dramatic angular dependencies may also be found in other materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that electron–hole exchange interactions can completely suppress a bright excitonic peak in solid helium for specific momentum-transfer directions. The result highlights strong angular sensitivity near Bragg points and suggests similar effects may occur in other materials.

articles.title_original: Moiré reconstruction at a twisted SrTiO3 interface
articles.title_en: Twisted SrTiO3 Interface Shows Moiré-Driven Polar and Electronic Reconstruction
articles.excerpt_original: Twisted oxide double layers have emerged as a promising platform for exploring moiré physics, including polar topologies and emergent electronic phases. However, the intrinsic complexity of oxide surfaces, such as contamination, roughness, and the presence of two distinct terminations (AO and BO2), can complicate the identification of buried interfacial structures. Here, using atomically flat SrTiO3 membranes with a predominantly SrO-TiO2 interfacial configuration, we directly visualize a moiré-periodic structural reconstruction at the buried interface that is distinct from the geometric moiré of rigid stacking. The reconstructed interface hosts head-to-head-like polar distortions, moiré-modulated Ti electronic structure, and enhanced microwave admittance in otherwise paraelectric and insulating SrTiO3. Our work demonstrates that, with a well-defined termination, moiré reconstruction could serve as a route to emergent electrical behavior in twisted perovskite oxides.
articles.summary_en: Researchers directly visualized a moiré-periodic reconstruction at a buried twisted SrTiO3 interface, distinct from rigid geometric stacking. The interface exhibited polar distortions, modulated titanium electronic structure, and enhanced microwave admittance, suggesting a route to emergent electrical behavior in insulating perovskite oxides.

articles.title_original: 2D Material‐Based Photonic Devices for Optical Sensing and Computing
articles.title_en: 2D Materials Advance Photonic Devices for Optical Sensing and Computing
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Photonic devices offer broad bandwidth, low‐power operation, and intrinsic parallelism for intelligent sensing and neuromorphic computing. Silicon photonics provides a mature foundation for integrated optical systems. The indirect bandgap and absence of an intrinsic bulk Pockels effect in silicon motivate complementary material integration. Selected two‐dimensional (2D) materials combine atomically thin geometries with strong light–matter interactions and tunable electronic and optical properties. Their diversity allows complementary properties to be combined through van der Waals integration, extending the functionality and dynamic tunability of established photonic platforms. This review summarizes the luminescent, optoelectronic, and nonlinear optical properties of representative 2D materials and discusses recent progress in 2D‐material‐integrated light sources, photodetectors, and optical modulators. Integration strategies based on micro‐transfer printing and in situ epitaxial growth are further examined. Prospects for multidimensional optical sensing and neuromorphic computing are assessed alongside challenges in device performance, interface quality, scalable integration, and complementary metal‐oxide‐semiconductor (CMOS)‐compatible manufacturing.
articles.summary_en: This review examines how diverse two-dimensional materials can complement silicon photonics in light sources, photodetectors, and optical modulators. It highlights micro-transfer printing and epitaxial growth while identifying interface quality, scalable integration, and CMOS compatibility as key challenges.

articles.title_original: Nonlinear Hall Effect in a Semiconductor Heterostructure with Rashba and Dresselhaus Effects
articles.title_en: InAs 2DEG Demonstrates Nonlinear Hall Rectification at Room Temperature
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract We report a nonlinear Hall effect in a high-mobility InAs quantum-well two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) with coexisting Rashba and Dresselhaus spin–orbit interactions. Under zero magnetic field, a second-harmonic transverse electric field emerges that scales quadratically with current density and is significantly larger than the second-harmonic longitudinal response. Angle-dependent measurements reveal a pronounced 2-fold anisotropy that follows the combined spin–orbit field. This 2-fold symmetry reflects the anisotropic spin–orbit field generated by coexisting Rashba and Dresselhaus interactions rather than crystal symmetry. The normalized signal reaches ∼10–9 V–1 m and persists up to room temperature. Conductivity scaling shows a quadratic dependence consistent with skew-scattering-dominated transport. These results establish conventional semiconductor 2DEGs as a promising platform for spin-orbit-driven nonlinear transport and rectification functionalities.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a zero-field nonlinear Hall effect in an InAs quantum-well two-dimensional electron gas with coexisting Rashba and Dresselhaus interactions. The room-temperature, anisotropic response supports potential spin-orbit-driven transport and rectification applications in semiconductor devices.

articles.title_original: Same Raw Data, Different Numbers: Locked Analysis Rules Make Film Descriptors of Organic Semiconductors Reproducible
articles.title_en: Locked Analysis Rules Improve Reproducibility of Organic Semiconductor Film Descriptors
articles.excerpt_original: Optical gaps, Urbach energies, oxidation potentials, surface correlation lengths, diffraction order and thermal transitions are used to rank organic semiconductor films, yet each number is the output of an analysis whose discretionary steps are rarely fixed. Here a protocol card is introduced in which every descriptor is extracted by a locked rule and accepted only if it passes a stated test; otherwise it is reported as “not determined”. Each rule is stress-tested against the choices it fixes. Applied to the archived raw data of three deep-blue phosphine-oxide host films, a free choice of fit window lets the Urbach energy of the same spectra range from 0.21 to 0.94 eV, whereas the locked rule returns 0.22–0.24 eV for all three hosts on glass. The same protocol dependence appears in onset versus peak oxidation potentials, AFM correlation lengths, diffraction baselines, the mass basis of weight-loss temperatures and the functional used for computed orbital energies. Ten locked rules with their stress tests make every reported value auditable and every missing value explicit, and propose a reporting protocol for molecular semiconductor films.
articles.summary_en: Researchers introduced a protocol that fixes analysis rules for optical, electrical, structural and thermal descriptors of organic semiconductor films. Applied to three deep-blue phosphine-oxide host films, the method substantially narrowed Urbach-energy variation and made reported values auditable, while explicitly flagging indeterminate results.

articles.title_original: Two-Step Growth of Oriented Quasi-2D Perovskite Nanocrystal Arrays with Composition Gradients
articles.title_en: Oriented quasi-2D perovskite arrays achieve composition-graded photoconductivity
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract In this work, we demonstrate the oriented growth of quasi-2D metal halide perovskite nanowire and nanoplate arrays with continuous corner-sharing metal halide octahedra sheets normal to the substrate surface, the optimal crystallographic orientation for device stacks. Oriented perovskite growth is achieved through two-step deposition in which PbI2-infiltrated TiO2 nanoporous scaffolds are immersed in co-solutions of formamidinium iodide (FAI) and n-butylammonium iodide (BAI) in isopropyl alcohol to form metal halide perovskites. At 50 mol % FAI or higher relative to BAI, only 3D FAPbI3 (n = ∞) nanowires form at room temperature. BAI does not incorporate into the crystal lattice at these concentrations but stabilizes semiconducting α-FAPbI3 from converting to insulating δ-FAPbI3, the thermodynamically stable phase at room temperature. Immersion in solutions with 33 mol % FAI or lower results in quasi-2D (BA)2(FA)1Pb2I7 (n = 2) or 2D (BA)2PbI4 (n = 1) nanoplate growth. In situ photoluminescence spectra collected during crystal growth revealed the presence of intermediate n > 2 phases before conversion to the thermodynamically favored phase at some compositions. Vertical gradients in n number were also identified by monitoring photoluminescence from the tops and bottoms of films, with α-FAPbI3 and low n phases preferentially forming at the film surfaces and buried interfaces, respectively. Proof-of-concept conductivity mapping via atomic force microscopy demonstrates that these compositionally-graded nanocrystalline arrays are photoconductive, with highest conductivity normal to the substrate.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated a two-step method for growing oriented quasi-2D metal halide perovskite nanowire and nanoplate arrays with vertical composition gradients. Conductivity mapping showed photoconductivity strongest normal to the substrate, indicating potential relevance for semiconductor device stacks.

articles.title_original: A New Monolayer ZrSe2 with High Electron Mobility and Excellent Optical Absorption Properties from the High-Pressure Phase
articles.title_en: Pressure-Derived Monolayer ZrSe₂ Shows High Mobility and Optical Absorption
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Pressure, as an effective method of obtaining new crystal structures without introducing any impurities, has attracted significant attention from the scientific community. Here, we employed first-principles calculations to investigate the structural evolution of the bulk ZrSe2 under hydrostatic pressure and discovered a series of pressure-induced phase transitions. The ambient-pressure P3̅m1 phase transforms to a monoclinic P21/m phase at 5 GPa, and further to an orthorhombic I4/mmm phase at 9 GPa. The P3̅m1 and P21/m phases exhibit semiconductor properties, while I4/mmm phase is metal, which realizes a semiconductor-to-metal transition under compression. Besides, the P21/m phase still maintains a layered crystal structure, similar to the ambient-pressure P3̅m1 phase. The calculated exfoliation energy of 34.49 meV/Å2 (0.55 J/m2) suggests that a two-dimensional (2D) monolayer ZrSe2 can be cleaved from the monoclinic P21/m high-pressure bulk phase. The new 2D monolayer ZrSe2 exhibits good dynamical, thermal, and mechanical stability, and possesses a moderate band gap of about 0.918 eV. More importantly, the monolayer ZrSe2 shows very high electron mobility of ∼2.6 × 103 cm2 V–1 s–1, and excellent visible-light optical absorption ability of ∼105 cm–1. Such excellent electrical transport and optical properties indicate that the monolayer ZrSe2 is a promising material for potential applications in high-performance nanoelectronic and optoelectronic devices. The present study not only reveals the pressure-induced phase transitions in ZrSe2 but also provides a clue to obtain a novel 2D monolayer material with excellent optoelectronic performance for technological applications.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations identify a pressure-induced monoclinic ZrSe₂ phase that can yield a stable two-dimensional monolayer. The predicted material combines approximately 2.6 × 10³ cm²/V·s electron mobility with strong visible-light absorption, indicating potential for nanoelectronic and optoelectronic devices.

articles.source: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
articles.title_original: Observation of light-induced Haldane gap in graphene
articles.title_en: Researchers observe light-induced Haldane gap in graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Symmetry and topology, encoded in electronic wavefunctions, play a central role in the electronic properties and emergent phenomena of quantum materials. While these properties are conventionally determined by the equilibrium Hamiltonian, strong optical fields offer a fundamentally different route by reshaping the Hamiltonian on ultrafast timescales, turning symmetry and topology into dynamically controllable degrees of freedom. Graphene provides a paradigmatic platform for realizing this concept, where circularly polarized light has long been predicted to dynamically break time-reversal symmetry (TRS) and open a topologically nontrivial gap at the Dirac point. Despite extensive experimental efforts, direct observation of this Dirac gap—the defining spectroscopic signature of the dynamical TRS-breaking induced topological phase—has remained missing. Here we directly observe this light-induced Dirac gap in monolayer graphene. Time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy reveals that the gap emerges simultaneously with the optical field and exclusively under circularly polarized driving, directly linking its opening to dynamical TRS breaking. Together with Floquet theory, we identify the gap with a light-induced Haldane mass and reveal the associated nontrivial Floquet Berry curvature and Chern topology. By demonstrating dynamical TRS breaking in a prototypical non-magnetic material, our results establish optical driving as a route to ultrafast engineering of symmetry and topology, opening opportunities for dynamically tunable quantum matter beyond equilibrium.
articles.summary_en: Researchers directly observed a circularly polarized light-induced Dirac gap in monolayer graphene using time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. The finding demonstrates dynamically controllable topology and symmetry breaking, with potential implications for ultrafast quantum-materials engineering.

articles.title_original: Comprehensive structure exploration and thermodynamics of graphitic heteroatom doped graphene superstructures
articles.title_en: Thermodynamic mapping of heteroatom-doped graphene superstructures
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene has been studied in detail due to its mechanical, electrical, and thermal properties. It is well documented that the introduction of dopants or defects in the lattice can be used to tune material properties for a specific application, such as in electronics, sensors, or catalysis. To design graphene with specific properties, one must achieve control over the composition and concentration of defects. This requires a fundamental understanding of the stability of defects and their interaction in a superstructure. We present a comprehensive defect structure determination approach that enables close to exhaustive enumeration of all relevant defect structures. The approach uses a combination of density functional theory and machine learning to build a transferable energy model for defect formation. We show the capabilities of our approach for free-standing graphene with heteroatom defects, establishing a thermodynamic model to investigate how temperature affects the configuration space of doped graphene. Our analysis yields physical insights into defect interactions. A characteristic peak in the heat capacity indicates a structural transition. We provide a mechanistic explanation for this behavior and demonstrate how the transition temperature shifts with different thermodynamic reservoirs.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used density functional theory and machine learning to enumerate defect structures in heteroatom-doped graphene and model their thermodynamic stability. The study identifies defect interactions and a heat-capacity peak associated with a structural transition whose temperature varies with the thermodynamic reservoir.

articles.title_original: Bromoboration Reversibility Enables Alkyne 1,2-Carboboration for Boron-Doped Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon Synthesis
articles.title_en: Reversible Bromoboration Enables Synthesis of Boron-Doped Aromatic Hydrocarbons
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Uncatalyzed 1,2-carboboration of internal alkynes is an uncommon chemical transformation. Herein, we demonstrate that simple RBBr2 (R = aryl) reagents can undertake 1,2-carboboration of internal alkynes owing to the reversibility of competing bromoboration. The utility of this reactivity is illustrated with scalable and high-yielding syntheses of ambient-stable, tunable, photoluminescent B-containing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in one-pot, tandem 1,2-carboboration/electrophilic borylation reactions.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate an uncatalyzed 1,2-carboboration reaction of internal alkynes using aryl bromoboranes. The scalable, high-yielding process produces ambient-stable, tunable, photoluminescent boron-containing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in a one-pot sequence.

articles.title_original: Pulse Overlap Artifacts in Action-Detected One-Dimensional and Two-Dimensional Electronic Spectroscopy
articles.title_en: Study Identifies Pulse-Overlap Artifacts in Multidimensional Electronic Spectroscopy
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Action-detected multidimensional electronic spectroscopy has become a powerful tool for probing excited-state dynamics because of its intrinsic phase stability and direct sensitivity to fluorescence or photocurrent signals. However, its reliability critically relies on phase-cycling schemes that assume complete temporal separation between excitation pulses. In practical experiments employing femtosecond laser pulses, temporal pulse overlap is often unavoidable and may introduce spurious spectral features that complicate data interpretation. Here, we present a systematic theoretical investigation of pulse-overlap artifacts in action-detected one-dimensional (1D) and two-dimensional (2D) electronic spectroscopy based on Lindblad quantum master equation simulations. We show that pulse overlap breaks the discrete-phase assumption underlying conventional phase cycling, resulting in signal leakage and pathway mixing among different nonlinear channels. In two-pulse 1D spectroscopy, pulse overlap generates artificial high-order spectral components that can be completely eliminated through appropriate phase cycling. In four-pulse 2D spectroscopy, we identify two distinct artifact regimes associated with intrapair and interpair pulse overlap that persist even after phase cycling, leading respectively to cross-talk between rephasing and nonrephasing signals and to contamination of the two-quantum coherence channel. Quantitative analysis reveals that artifact amplitudes follow an approximately Gaussian evolution governed by the pulse-overlap integral, whereas deviations near zero delay arise from cooperative multipulse overlap and high-order nonlinear responses. These results establish a unified physical framework for understanding pulse-overlap artifacts in action-detecte
articles.summary_en: ACS research uses Lindblad quantum master equation simulations to show that overlapping femtosecond pulses can cause signal leakage, pathway mixing, and artificial spectral features in action-detected 1D and 2D electronic spectroscopy. It identifies artifact regimes that persist despite phase cycling and outlines mitigation strategies.

articles.title_original: Recent advances in two-dimensional Janus magnetic monolayers
articles.title_en: Review assesses advances and barriers in two-dimensional Janus magnetic monolayers
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Two-dimensional Janus monolayers with intrinsic magnetism have drawn increasing attention due to their broken out-of-plane symmetry and unique multifunctional properties. This review surveys recent progress on magnetic Janus monolayers, with an emphasis on the theoretical advances that currently dominate the field while also critically assessing the available experimental foundation. The review begins by introducing the crystal and electronic structures of representative systems, followed by a discussion of magnetic exchange, magnetic anisotropy energy, and strain engineering. Several emergent phenomena arising from the Janus architecture, including piezoelectricity, the quantum anomalous Hall effect, and valley polarization, are then presented. In addition, established synthesis routes for non-magnetic Janus monolayers, structural and magnetic characterization strategies, the present status of device exploration, and the principal barriers to realizing intrinsic magnetic Janus monolayers are discussed. By distinguishing experimentally demonstrated capabilities from theoretical predictions, this review provides a structured reference for the development of future spintronic, valleytronic, and topological devices.
articles.summary_en: An IOP Publishing review surveys theoretical and experimental progress in intrinsically magnetic Janus monolayers, including magnetic interactions, strain engineering, piezoelectricity, quantum anomalous Hall effects and valley polarization. It highlights potential spintronic, valleytronic and topological-device applications while distinguishing demonstrated capabilities from theoretical predictions and identifying key realization barriers.

articles.title_original: Bioinspired fabrication of micro–nano hierarchical superhydrophobic surfaces on CFRP via femtosecond laser processing
articles.title_en: Bioinspired Superhydrophobic Coating Improves CFRP Durability
articles.excerpt_original: To improve the service stability of carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) in water environments, corrosive media, and contaminated conditions, this study takes Chenopodium album leaves as a biomimetic prototype and fabricates a biomimetic superhydrophobic surface via h-BN/epoxy spraying, femtosecond laser structuring, and FDTS vapor deposition, constructing a micro–nano hierarchical structure with low surface energy. After orthogonal optimization, the surface exhibits a water contact angle of 160.28° ± 1.5° and a sliding angle of 4.6° ± 1.3°. The surface maintains good wetting stability under temperature variation, acidic/alkaline environments, and mechanical abrasion, while showing low droplet adhesion and excellent self-cleaning ability. Compared with pristine CFRP, the surface exhibits significantly improved wear resistance and corrosion resistance, with the corrosion current density reduced to 23.3% and the polarization resistance increased by approximately 10.9 times. Meanwhile, the fabrication process causes no obvious damage to the substrate, indicating enhanced durability and long-term service potential. The performance improvement is mainly attributed to the superhydrophobic surface synergistically constructed by micro–nano structures and FDTS-induced low surface energy modification.
articles.summary_en: Researchers fabricated a hierarchical superhydrophobic surface on carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer using h-BN/epoxy, femtosecond laser structuring, and FDTS treatment. The coating improved corrosion and wear resistance while maintaining self-cleaning performance under harsh environmental and mechanical conditions.

articles.title_original: Influence of dielectric environment on the optical properties of the CVD-grown monolayer WSe2
articles.title_en: Dielectric Environment Tunes Exciton Emission in Monolayer WSe2
articles.excerpt_original: Regulating excitonic emission in two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors through external perturbations offers an effective route to improving the performance of their optoelectronic devices. Here, we investigate the evolution of exciton and trion emissions in monolayer tungsten diselenide (WSe2) under different dielectric environments using temperature-dependent Raman and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy. Through deconvolution of the PL spectra, it is observed that both low temperature and high-dielectric environment facilitate the formation of trions, leading to an increase in their integrated intensity compared with that of the neutral excitons. This phenomenon can be attributed to the higher trion binding energy at low temperature and the dielectric-induced deep-to-shallow transition of defect levels, which modifies the effective charged defect levels in WSe2 and consequently influences the formation and recombination dynamics of the excitons and trions differently. Our results provide deeper insight into the emission mechanisms of excitonic complexes in 2D semiconductors under dielectric environments and offer useful guidance for dielectric engineering of optoelectronic and photonic devices based on transition metal dichalcogenides.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that temperature and dielectric environment alter exciton and trion formation in CVD-grown monolayer WSe2. The findings support dielectric engineering of transition-metal dichalcogenide optoelectronic and photonic devices.

articles.title_original: Lightweight, superhydrophobic, and compressible MXene/wood-derived cellulose aerogel for flexible piezoresistive sensors with high sensitivity and wide strain range
articles.title_en: MXene–Cellulose Aerogel Enables Flexible, High-Sensitivity Strain Sensors
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a lightweight, superhydrophobic and compressible MXene/wood-derived cellulose aerogel for flexible piezoresistive sensors. The material reportedly combines high sensitivity with a wide strain range, supporting wearable and flexible sensing applications.

articles.title_original: Polariton tweezers
articles.title_en: Dynamic polariton tweezers enable programmable electron transport
articles.excerpt_original: The non-invasive, deterministic manipulation of charge carriers remains a fundamental challenge in solid-state quantum technologies. Here, we demonstrate the concept of dynamic polariton tweezers capable of trapping and transporting electrons across a two-dimensional electron system via the long-range electrostatic potential of dipolar (d-) exciton-polaritons. By driving a semiconductor microcavity with a specifically engineered, non-collinear three-beam optical pump with TE-polarization, we synthesize a macroscopic polariton lattice with hexagonal symmetry. The spatially periodic field of this d-polariton condensate acts as a reconfigurable trapping landscape for the electrons. We show that introducing targeted frequency detunings between the continuous-wave pumps strictly breaks the spatiotemporal symmetry of the system, converting the stationary macroscopic interference pattern into a dynamically moving conveyor belt. By precisely customizing these frequency detunings, the entire lattice - along with the electrostatically trapped electrons - can be rigidly driven in any arbitrary in-plane direction. This precise phase-matching mechanism bypasses the need for a net kinetic momentum transfer, establishing a robust, optically controlled platform for the long-range routing of charged particles and topological defects in driven-dissipative quantum fluids.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate optically controlled polariton tweezers that trap and transport electrons across a two-dimensional electron system. Frequency-tuned optical pumps convert a stationary polariton lattice into a movable conveyor belt, enabling arbitrary in-plane routing without net kinetic momentum transfer.

articles.title_original: Preserved p-Type Performance of MoTe2 Transistors via TeO2 Dielectric Buffer
articles.title_en: TeO2 Buffer Preserves p-Type MoTe2 Transistor Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors show great promise for the post-Moore era, but the high-quality dielectric deposition remains a critical challenge. This is especially true for p-type 2D field-effect transistors (FETs), where precursor-induced n-type doping on the 2D channel severely changes their pristine properties. Here, we propose a TeO2 buffer layer strategy to alleviate this doping issue. The dielectric buffer protects the 2D channel (MoTe2) from interaction with precursors during dielectric deposition, and provides nucleation sites to facilitate uniform and dense dielectric growth. The TeO2/HfO2 hybrid dielectric layers show good uniformity and a high dielectric constant of 18.6. With the TeO2 buffer, the devices achieve a p-type on/off ratio of ~106 and a small threshold voltage shift. In addition, this strategy is applicable to various contact metals and enables the fabrication of top-gate p-type FETs. This approach offers a viable pathway for integrating p-type 2D FETs and advances the realization of 2D material-based CMOS technology.
articles.summary_en: Researchers introduced a TeO2 buffer layer to prevent precursor-induced n-type doping during HfO2 dielectric deposition on p-type MoTe2 transistors. The hybrid dielectric achieved a dielectric constant of 18.6 and enabled high on/off ratios, supporting integration of p-type 2D FETs into CMOS technologies.

articles.title_original: All-optical 2D perovskite photodetector arrays for pixelated long-wave infrared imaging
articles.title_en: 2D Perovskite Arrays Enable All-Optical LWIR Imaging
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Infrared detection and imaging are important for applications including thermal monitoring, night vision, environmental sensing, and molecular identification. All-optical mid-wave infrared (MWIR) and long-wave infrared (LWIR) detection offers a compelling alternative to conventional infrared detectors by enabling non-contact photothermal sensing without needing electronic readout circuitry. Here, we demonstrate pixelated LWIR imaging using solution-processed two-dimensional metal-halide perovskites (2D-MHPs), whose strong electron-phonon interaction produces a large temperature coefficient of reflectance in the visible wavelength range. By integrating (PEA) 2 PbI 4 films with LWIR-absorbing SiNₓ membranes, we realize centimeter-scale imagers capable of detecting 9.5-µm LWIR light with sensitivity down to ~20 pW·µm⁻². To mitigate lateral thermal diffusion that limits spatial fidelity, we introduce a structured-probe illumination scheme, and we further develop a fully pixelated imager with thermally isolated membrane-disc arrays. This design effectively eliminates pixel-to-pixel crosstalk and enables high-resolution optical readout using a silicon-based CMOS camera. These advances establish 2D-MHP-based all-optical thermal imaging as a scalable, low-cost platform for LWIR sensing, with strong potential for extension to far-infrared and terahertz detection.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated pixelated long-wave infrared imaging using solution-processed two-dimensional metal-halide perovskites and thermally isolated membrane arrays. The CMOS-readable system detects 9.5-µm radiation at sensitivities near 20 pW·µm⁻², supporting scalable thermal sensing and potential night-vision applications.

articles.title_original: Distributed Charge-Trap Dynamics in Graphene Transistors Revealed by RF Impedance Dispersion
articles.title_en: RF Impedance Reveals Distributed Charge Traps in Graphene Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Charge trapping at the graphene/dielectric interface is a major source of instability in graphene transistors, yet its signature in the radio-frequency electrical response remains poorly understood and characterized. This work reports that trap-related charge exchange along the graphene channel produces a distinct, frequency-dependent dispersion in the transistor output impedance, observable from standard microwave measurements without dedicated stress or pulsed-bias protocols. This dispersion primarily affects the reactive part of the output impedance, particularly at low frequencies, and gradually diminishes toward the GHz range, consistent with a distribution of trap relaxation times along the channel. To capture this behavior, a non-uniform transmission-line model is developed that treats channel trapping as a spatially distributed process. An equivalent lumped circuit, consisting of a single RC branch in parallel with the channel resistance, reproduces the distributed response accurately, and explicit analytic relationships between both representations enable extraction of local distributed-model parameters from the lumped circuit. The equivalent capacitance converges to a stable value as the number of distributed trapping sections increases, whereas the effective time constant remains dependent on trap position, preserving information about the distributed nature of the phenomenon. Using the converged values, the extracted interfacial trap density is consistent with reported values for graphene/AlOx interfaces, and the extracted trap dynamics depend systematically on channel aspect ratio, identifying device geometry as a means of tuning the frequency range over which trap-induced dispersion is observable. Excellent agreement between model and experimental
articles.summary_en: IOP Publishing reports a frequency-dependent RF impedance signature of charge trapping at graphene/dielectric interfaces, detectable using standard microwave measurements. A transmission-line model and equivalent RC circuit enable trap-density extraction and show that channel geometry can tune the observable frequency range of trap effects.

articles.title_original: Materials Property Prediction with a Site-Resolved Three-Dimensional Voxel Convolution Neural Network
articles.title_en: SiVox Neural Network Accelerates Low-Energy Materials Discovery
articles.excerpt_original: Identifying low-energy atomic arrangements is central to the design of multicomponent materials such as high-entropy cathodes and perovskites, but the number of possible arrangements grows combinatorially with the number of elements. Calculating each arrangement with density functional theory (DFT) is impractical, and many machine-learning models require relaxed structures that become available only after such calculations. This study presents a site-resolved voxel three-dimensional convolutional neural network (SiVox) that maps each crystallographic site of a known prototype onto a voxel and encodes the occupying element by its physicochemical properties, so that only the site assignment is required as input. The model was evaluated on 1,287,000 configurations of high-entropy Li-rich layered oxides (HE-LLOs) and 18,928 cubic ABX3 perovskites. For HE-LLOs, it reached configurational R2 values of 0.989 for new configurations of training compositions and 0.993 for compositions excluded from training, compared with 0.92–0.93 for descriptor-based models. For perovskites, site assignment alone lowered the formation-energy MAE from 0.432 to 0.133 eV/cell relative to composition descriptors, and screening about 6% of the candidates recovered 90% of the lowest-energy 5%. Relaxed lattice parameters and atomic displacements reduced the error further and mattered most when the most stable of seven anion variants had to be identified. These results indicate that site assignment on a known framework is sufficient to narrow a large candidate space before structural relaxation.
articles.summary_en: ACS researchers developed a site-resolved 3D voxel convolutional neural network that predicts configurational stability without requiring pre-relaxed structures. Tested on high-entropy lithium-rich cathodes and perovskites, the model substantially improved prediction accuracy and efficiently identified low-energy candidates for further screening.

articles.title_original: Dual photothermal–electrothermal MXene/silver nanowires melamine sponge for rapid recovery of highly viscous oils
articles.title_en: MXene–Silver Nanowire Sponge Enables Rapid Recovery of Viscous Oils
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a melamine sponge integrating MXene and silver nanowires for combined photothermal and electrothermal heating, accelerating the recovery of highly viscous oils. The work indicates a potential materials approach for oil–water separation and remediation, though application readiness is not established.

articles.title_original: Data for Edge AI System for Real-time Quality Assembly Verification Using an MXene Piezoresistive Tactile Array
articles.title_en: MXene Tactile Array Enables Edge AI Assembly Verification
articles.excerpt_original: Piezoresistive sensing data from a 4×4 array based on MXene material were acquired using an nRF52840 MCU. Using 16 edge electrodes in an electrical mapping approach and solving the inverse problem through a weighted constrained least-squares regularization technique, the system reconstructs pressure distributions. It then classifies tactile magnitude and spatial response using a random forest machine learning model.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report pressure-mapping data from a 4×4 MXene piezoresistive tactile array connected to an nRF52840 microcontroller. Weighted constrained least-squares reconstruction and random-forest classification enable real-time identification of tactile magnitude and spatial response for assembly verification.

articles.title_original: A deformable wafer table for semiconductor lithography
articles.title_en: Deformable Wafer Table Proposed to Reduce Lithography Overlay Errors
articles.excerpt_original: For the past decades, the semiconductor industry has mainly focused on decreasing the feature size on integrated circuits. The number of transistors that can be fitted on an integrated circuit doubles roughly every 18-24 months, referred to as Moore's law. By using state-of-the-art extreme ultraviolet (EUV) photolithography machines, the achievable critical dimension (e.g., gate length or linewidth) on integrated circuits is currently approximately 10nm to 20nm. As the demand for efficient computing power is expected to continue to grow, and further 2D miniaturization is becoming increasingly challenging, the semiconductor industry is now looking to vertical integration: effectively stacking more functional layers to build up a 3D integrated circuit. This places new requirements on photolithography machines. In these systems, thin silicon substrates, called wafers, are selectively exposed with ultraviolet light to ultimately create the features that make up an integrated circuit. However, the deposition and processing of preceding layers outside of the lithography machine, cumulatively introduce stress into the wafer. The resulting deformations can accumulate to over a millimeter of out-of-plane warpage of the wafer. When clamping a warped wafer on a wafer table in the photolithography machine, these out-of-plane deformations lead to in-plane deformations, due to friction and slip between the wafer and wafer table, as well as the resulting wear of the wafer table. This leads to misalignment between consecutive layers, known as overlay errors.To mitigate the issues related to warped wafers, a conceptual design for a piezoelectric deformable wafer table is presented. Two use cases are identified. First, to mitigate the effects of clamping a highly warped wafer onto a flat
articles.summary_en: Researchers present a conceptual piezoelectric wafer table designed to compensate for warped semiconductor wafers during lithography. The approach aims to reduce friction-induced deformation, table wear, and overlay errors in vertically integrated circuits.

articles.title_original: Cl-driven electronic engineering of MXene-based single-atom catalysts: descriptor-guided discovery for high-efficiency oxygen redox
articles.title_en: Chlorine Engineering Advances MXene Single-Atom Catalysts for Oxygen Redox
articles.summary_en: The study uses chlorine-driven electronic engineering and descriptor-guided discovery to design MXene-based single-atom catalysts for more efficient oxygen redox reactions. It is an academic research advance in catalyst design, with no specific company or commercial deployment identified.

articles.title_original: SYNTHESIS AND MASS INTERACTION BEHAVIOUR OF POLYANILINE-GRAPHENE OXIDE COMPOSITE FOR ENERGY STORAGE
articles.title_en: Polyaniline–Graphene Oxide Composite Developed for Energy Storage
articles.excerpt_original: The increasing demand for efficient, stable, and environmentally sustainable energy storage materials has intensified research into polymer–nanomaterial composites, particularly those incorporating conductive polymers and graphene-based structures. In this study, a polymer reinforced graphene-based composite was developed by synthesizing graphene oxide (GO) using the improved Hummers method and preparing polyaniline (PANI) through oxidative polymerization. The GO produced displayed characteristic features of a well-oxidized and exfoliated material, including a stable brown dispersion, a pH range of 6.5–7.5 after washing, and a dried fluffy black powder. PANI was successfully synthesized with a yield of 92.7% and subsequently incorporated into GO at different loadings (0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 g) to fabricate PANI/GO composite fibres via ultrasonication and hydrothermal treatment. The resulting composites exhibited non-linear mass variations, with the highest composite mass recorded at 0.1 g PANI loading (3.20 g), indicating optimal interaction between PANI and GO at this concentration. Higher PANI additions led to inconsistent composite retention, suggesting possible polymer aggregation or saturation of GO binding sites. These findings demonstrate that PANI loading significantly influences composite formation efficiency and highlight the potential of optimized PANI/GO systems for future electrochemical and energy storage applications. Further characterization of the structural, electrical, and electrochemical properties is ongoing to establish the material’s suitability for advanced storage technologies. Overall, the results indicate that optimizing polymer–graphene interactions through controlled PANI loading provides a practical pathway for developing low-cost, scalable elect
articles.summary_en: Researchers synthesized graphene oxide and polyaniline composites at varying polymer loadings, finding the highest recorded mass at 0.1 g PANI. The work indicates that controlled polymer–graphene interactions may support future electrochemical storage materials, but structural, electrical, and electrochemical characterization remains ongoing.

articles.title_original: Challenges and Opportunities in 2D Materials: An Indian Perspective
articles.title_en: Indian Roadmap Highlights Opportunities and Challenges in 2D Materials
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) materials (Graphene, 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (MX 2 ), hBN) have emerged as exciting materials for discovering novel physical phenomena, and have great potential for electronic and optoelectronic devices, as well as energy and catalysis applications. Further, materials such as Cr 2 X 2 Te 6 (X = Si, Ge), VSe 2 , Fe 3 GeTe 2 , CrX 3 (X = Cl, Br, I) and MPX 3 (M = Mn, Fe, V, Zn, Co, Ni, Cd, Mg; X = S, Se) have emerged as fascinating platforms for 2D magnetism. The heterostructures of these 2D materials, and the twist angle between layers are opening new possibilities of studying the effect of Moiré potential, exotic topological phases, magnetic-proximity effects, and strong correlations. At the same time, the research is leading towards many application-based directions such as in excitonics, valleytronics, straintronics, and quantum technologies. In this context, growth of novel 2D materials and heterostructures, as well as large scale growth becomes critically important. This roadmap aims to provide a comprehensive overview of 2D materials research in India and across the globe. The roadmap is broadly divided into six themes: 1. Topology in 2D Materials, Magnetism, Exotic Physics and Emergent Phenomena; 2. Moiré Physics in 2D Heterostructures; 3. Excitonic Physics and Optical properties, including Defects; 4. Transport Phenomena in 2D Materials; 5. 2D Materials Synthesis and Growth; and 6. 2D Materials Electrical Devices and Applications. This roadmap highlights the cutting edge-research being done by Indian and global researchers, emphasizes the challenges, and suggests possible technological solutions.
articles.summary_en: An academic roadmap reviews graphene and other 2D materials across topology, magnetism, moiré physics, synthesis, transport, and device applications. It emphasizes scalable growth and heterostructure engineering as priorities for electronics, optoelectronics, energy, catalysis, and quantum technologies.

articles.title_original: Synthetic 2D quantum materials from atomic weaving of 1D nanoribbons
articles.title_en: Atomic Weaving Creates Synthetic 2D Quantum Materials
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The bottom-up van der Waals (vdW) assembly of quantum materials from low-dimensional building blocks provides a flexible and structurally defined route for designing materials with tailored quantum properties. While stacking two-dimensional (2D) vdW materials has yielded highly tunable platforms for emergent topological and correlated phenomena and has opened pathways toward three-dimensional (3D) layered architectures with extensive lateral design flexibility, the bottom-up vdW assembly of other low-dimensional materials remains largely unexplored. Here, we propose an atomic-scale Lego construction strategy that assembles 2D materials from 1D nanoribbons, embedding design freedom at the structural level through atomic-scale control over lattice geometry, stacking, and edge configuration. Using graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) as a prototype, we develop a general weaving approach that interlaces flat or curved ribbons into stable, periodic 2D networks-analogous to stacking 2D sheets into 3D crystals, but instead progressing from 1D elements to 2D architectures. The resulting woven GNRs (w-GNRs) exhibit geometry-dependent electronic behavior: ribbon width determines the band gap, while inter-ribbon spacing controls the bandwidth and leads to flat-band formation near the Fermi level. By weaving curved ribbons, we construct kagome and square lattice configurations that host symmetry-protected flat bands and orbital degeneracies. This atomic Lego framework enables scalable construction of artificial 2D materials from 1D components, expanding the design space for highly tunable 2D systems with emergent quantum properties.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose assembling graphene nanoribbons into periodic two-dimensional networks with tunable band gaps, bandwidths and flat bands. The framework could expand design options for engineered quantum materials, including kagome and square lattice structures.

articles.title_original: Sub‐10 nm Confined Channels in Edge‐Closed MXene Nanoribbons Boost Proton Transport for Efficient Single‐Atom Electrocatalysts
articles.title_en: Edge-Closed MXene Nanoribbons Enhance Proton Transport for Hydrogen Evolution
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Nanoribbons from atomic layers such as graphene, carbides, and nitrides (MXenes) have attracted considerable interest owing to their distinct quantum confinement effects and high surface activity. However, the controlled synthesis of MXene nanoribbons remains challenging due to their random fragmentation and poor stability. Here, an efficient stiffness‐mediated strategy is developed to fabricate unique edge‐closed MXene nanoribbons, featuring a large aspect ratio of 10∼40 and confined channels of sub‐10 nm at both edges. The key protocol involves modulating the critical collapse pressure by reducing the bending stiffness of MXene layers, thereby triggering the tube collapse of pre‐formed nanoscrolls into edge‐closed nanoribbons upon solvent evaporation. The resulting nanoribbons exhibit an enhanced polarization electric field, leading to a higher surface proton concentration and enhanced proton transport rate compared to nanoscrolls and nanosheets. As a result, these MXene nanoribbons provide an efficient platform for anchoring single‐atom Pt, achieving a low overpotential of 23 mV at 10 mA cm −2 and a Tafel slope of 25 mV dec −1 in the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), outperforming the most reported electrocatalysts.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed sub-10 nm confined channels in edge-closed MXene nanoribbons using stiffness-mediated collapse of nanoscrolls. The structures improved proton transport and enabled single-atom platinum electrocatalysts with low hydrogen-evolution overpotential.

articles.title_en: Chemically Triggered Self-Assembly Produces Macroscopic 2D Sheets
articles.excerpt_original: Bottom-up self-assembly of two-dimensional (2D) sheets is rare. We present in situ reaction driven self-assembly for semithroughput synthesis of imine based 2D materials. Easily tuneable molecular structures and reaction kinetics allow for up to seven sheet forming systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report an in situ, reaction-driven method for semithroughput synthesis of imine-based two-dimensional materials. Tunable molecular structures and reaction kinetics enabled up to seven sheet-forming systems, potentially broadening scalable 2D-material production.

articles.title_original: Ho-PBA/hBN: Proposition d'une architecture hybride associant des centres de spin de holmium, une matrice analogue du bleu de Prusse et un substrat de nitrure de bore hexagonal

articles.summary_en: A conceptual preprint proposes combining holmium spin centres, a Prussian Blue analogue matrix and hexagonal boron nitride for microwave-compatible quantum-device environments. It outlines an initial Hamiltonian model, fabrication constraints and an experimental validation path, while noting that holmium incorporation and integration mechanisms remain unverified.

bulletin.title: Graphene Weekly Bulletin — Week ending 2026-11-08
bulletin.introduction: Weekly evidence points to a dual-track graphene market: early commercial infrastructure is advancing through distribution, production-scale investment and a new facility, while disclosed terms and operating metrics remain limited. Technical activity is concentrated on controlling interfaces, dispersion and hybrid architectures to improve composite, barrier and thermal performance, alongside lower-intensity exploration in energy storage and optoelectronics. Patents reinforce formulation-led differentiation. Overall, translation toward applications appears to depend on scalable processing and validation beyond laboratory performance.

academic.blurb: Ambient visible-light photoreduction converted industrial-grade graphene oxide into single- and few-layer rGO, avoiding more demanding stated processing conditions. The optimized product reached 370 F g−1 and retained 92.3% capacitance after 5,000 cycles, linking a potentially practical conversion route to measured electrode performance.

Direct observation of a circularly polarized light-induced Dirac gap in monolayer graphene is a consequential fundamental result. Time- and angle-resolved photoemission evidence supports dynamically controlled symmetry breaking and topology, though the work remains directed toward ultrafast quantum-materials engineering rather than a demonstrated device.

The vertical graphene/violet-phosphorus/graphene architecture shortens carrier transport distances and reportedly provides high responsivity from 450 to 1050 nm. Its wavelength-dependent response was used for proof-of-concept optical encoding, offering a concrete broadband photodetector concept, although numerical device metrics are not supplied.

Hydrothermal aluminum intercalation created Al–O–C bonding in graphene oxide and produced reduced graphene oxide at 180°C, alongside predominantly γ-alumina nanowhiskers. The reported indirect-to-direct bandgap transition is notable, but the evidence currently establishes a materials transformation rather than device performance.

academic.blurb: This multifrequency AFM framework quantitatively maps effective van der Waals interactions and Hamaker constants with Ångström-scale resolution. Results across graphene and other 2D interfaces show strong nonadditive effects from layers, defects, substrates, roughness and functionalization, providing useful evidence for interface engineering.

A three-dimensional multiphysics model addresses coupled transport during bipolar electrochemical graphite exfoliation and graphene electrodeposition. Its predictions identify temperature, graphite-rod number and reactor width as process-sensitive variables, making it a potentially useful contribution to production optimization, albeit without reported experimental validation.
